articles.title: Rubio claims Strait of Hormuz oil flows near pre-war levels on some nights
articles.summary:
Rubio claims Strait of Hormuz oil flows near pre-war levels on some nights

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to more than four-fifths of their pre-war volume on some nights. He attributed the remaining shortfall to Iranian exports.

“Oil is getting out – on some nights it’s 80-85 percent of what was getting out pre-conflict.

“The only reason why it isn’t 100 percent is because Iranian oil isn’t getting out.

“The only oil that isn’t getting out consistently through the strait of Hormuz is the Iranian oil,” he told reporters at a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris.

Rubio said Washington would step up economic pressure on Tehran. “I have been told the economic campaign [against Iran] is working so well there’s no need for major combat operations,” he said.

“The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.

Rubio said Washington was “open to diplomacy” to end the war, but told reporters that “the Iranian demands are totally unrealistic. We expect that could change – and if it does, we’re prepared for diplomacy.”

He said Washington could forgo further strikes “if we’re achieving the same objectives through economic means”.

articles.title: ‘We woke up soaking wet’: Gaza’s displaced face another winter of floods and collapsed shelters
articles.summary:
‘We woke up soaking wet’: Gaza’s displaced face another winter of floods and collapsed shelters

Submitted by Ahmed Dremly on Tue, 11/10/2026 - 11:52
Heavy rains flood tents and threaten damaged buildings, leaving families with nowhere safe to go as Israel restricts humanitarian supplies
Displaced Palestinians at a partially flooded tent camp during a rainy day in Gaza City, 7 November 2026 (Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters)
Off

For the past four days, Nahla al-Majdoub, 48, and her family of eight have been staying with neighbours in the west of Gaza City after their tent was destroyed by the latest heavy rainfall.

Majdoub and her family had been sheltering in a makeshift tent at the port of Gaza for nearly two years after their home in the northern Gaza Strip was destroyed during Israel’s ground invasion.

But when heavy rain and strong winds swept across the besieged enclave last week, their fragile shelter could no longer protect them.

They were asleep when the storm began. They woke to the sound of thunder and rainwater pouring into their shelter, seeping through the roof and flooding the ground beneath their tent.

“I woke up soaking wet. I looked at my children, who were also wet and surrounded by water. We cried helplessly, not knowing what to do or how to protect them,” Majdoub said.

“I tried to collect the water inside the tent and push it outside, but it kept coming through the holes in the fabric and from underneath as the water continued to flood in.”

As the wind grew stronger, parts of the tent’s tarpaulin began to tear away. Fearing that the tent would collapse in the heavy rain while her young children were inside, Majdoub called on neighbours to help secure it and pile more sand around its edges.

But the situation deteriorated quickly.

“I decided to take my children and seek shelter in one of my neighbours’ stronger tents. As we were moving, the tarpaulin flew away and the tent collapsed while one of my daughters was still inside,” she said.

“All our clothes, mattresses and belongings were soaked. I stood in the rain, looking at the destroyed tent and everything we had lost, not knowing what to do.”

‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
Read More »

The family managed to retrieve their mattresses, but they remained wet. Majdoub said her children had been wearing the same wet clothes for four days because the few clothes they owned had all been soaked.

The flooding has added to the hardship Majdoub has faced since being wounded in an Israeli air strike in October 2025 while out shopping for her family.

“Shrapnel from the missile tore through my intestines. I underwent several surgeries, and the doctors told me they had fitted me with artificial intestines,” she said.

“I need regular medication that costs 170 shekels a week, which I have to take after eating, but I cannot afford it. I am always in pain, and the cold is making it worse.”

Majdoub is also worried about her seven-year-old daughter Aya, who has diabetes, as the family faces another winter without adequate shelter.

“We are a poor family. We cannot afford to buy another tent or tarpaulin every time a strong winter storm hits. Sometimes I have to ask neighbours to give us food for the children,” she said.

Majdoub and her family are staying with neighbours until the weather improves and they can try to rebuild their shelter.

“I am sorry that my family’s biggest dream now is just to have a strong tent that can withstand heavy rain and protect us from the cold,” she said.

‘We were soaked and unable to sleep'

For Sameh Doghomoush, 33, the latest storm exposed the limits of his attempts to protect his family from another winter in Gaza.

Doghomoush, his wife and their three sons live in their partially destroyed house in the al-Sabra neighbourhood, east of Gaza City.

Having experienced the previous winter, Doghomoush tried to prepare for the latest rainfall after learning about it on social media. He bought additional tarpaulins and spent two days securing openings in the roof and covering the building’s destroyed walls.

He and his wife Sana, 27, also placed basins and pots beneath the largest holes in the roof to catch the rainwater and prevent it from spreading through the house.

But their efforts failed within hours of the first rainfall.

“Rainwater flooded my house through the destroyed roof and broken windows. We were soaked and had to sit in the dark and wait until morning, unable to sleep,” he said.

“My three sons caught the cold, and with every new wave of rain, we all became ill.”

Doghomoush said his family had not received a tent or tarpaulin since the war began, despite their urgent need for shelter materials.

“Perhaps the priority is given to people living out in the streets, but we also need help. The crossings must be opened and more urgent supplies allowed into Gaza so that we can protect ourselves and our children from the winter,” he said.

Before the war, Doghomoush said, his home measured 180 square metres. He also owned a fish restaurant and a car, all of which were lost during Israel's three-year war.

He has since spent his savings on food, transport, firewood, tarpaulins and other basic necessities to survive.

“I used to buy my children new clothes and devices and take them to amusement parks. Now they ask for ordinary things such as new clothes, food and books for school, and I cannot afford them. They miss having a normal life,” he said.

“I tell them that I will bring them everything in the future, while I think inside that I am not even able to protect them from the cold winter.”

Doghomoush fears that he and his family could be trapped if their weakened building collapses, leaving them without shelter or putting their lives at risk.

“We are exhausted by this life and by facing death through bombardment, starvation, helplessness and now cold. I appeal to international organisations and governments around the world to help end our suffering by pressuring Israel to allow the entry of basic equipment to rebuild Gaza, and to ensure that we and our children receive our basic right to shelter.”

Tens of thousands of tents flooded

The Gaza Government Media Office said that more than 70,000 tents sheltering hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians had been flooded during the first 12 hours of the latest storm.

“Sand embankments had collapsed and dozens of cracked walls had fallen on displaced people, killing five people, wounding dozens more, while two people remain missing. The initial financial losses are estimated at more than $3m,” the media office told Middle East Eye.

'All our clothes, mattresses and belongings were soaked. I stood in the rain, looking at the destroyed tent and everything we had lost, not knowing what to do'

- Nahla al-Majdoub, displaced Palestinian

It also warned that “dozens of buildings, partially destroyed by years of intense Israeli bombardment, were now at risk of collapse as rainwater saturated the ground beneath them”.

“Israel had systematically destroyed more than 90 percent of Gaza’s infrastructure, including sewage networks, forcing Palestinians to crowd into dangerous areas where displacement camps had become increasingly exposed to flooding and other hazards.”

The office added that the destruction of infrastructure, combined with restrictions on the entry of shelter materials and other essential supplies, had made the humanitarian situation increasingly difficult as winter approached.

It said municipal and civil defence teams were working to respond to the damage but faced severe shortages of equipment and resources, alongside a huge gap between the amount of humanitarian aid entering Gaza and the actual needs of displaced people.

The office called on the international community to move beyond statements of condemnation and take action to secure the opening of crossings and the continuous entry of humanitarian supplies.

“Gaza urgently needed more than 100,000 new tents capable of withstanding harsh winter conditions, in addition to tens of thousands of mobile homes and temporary housing units and the entry of materials and equipment needed to repair infrastructure, sewage networks and rainwater drainage systems.”

Israel's political calculation

Palestinian political analyst and researcher Talal Abu Rokbeh said Israel is continuing to exert pressure on Palestinians in Gaza by worsening humanitarian conditions, including restricting the entry of essential shelter and protection supplies.

'I used to buy my children new clothes and take them to amusement parks. Now they ask for ordinary things and I cannot afford them'

- Hamed Doghomoush, displaced Palestinian

“The international community bears part of the responsibility because of its silence and its failure to hold Israel accountable or exert pressure on it to ensure the entry of humanitarian aid and provide protection,” Abu Rokbeh told MEE.

“Israel is seeking to frame the Palestinian cause as a humanitarian crisis rather than a political question concerning a people striving to exercise their right to self-determination, achieve national independence and establish an independent state.

“Israel is attempting to shift the world's attention towards the humanitarian dimension at the expense of the political one, rather than addressing the issue as a political question that requires a political solution.”

Abu Rokbeh added that the seriousness of any shift in US policy in the coming period should be measured by concrete developments on the ground.

These include whether the Palestinian technocratic committee is enabled to assume its responsibilities in Gaza, whether an international stabilisation force is deployed, and whether Israel is compelled to withdraw from the areas it has recently occupied, which account for 70 percent of the Gaza Strip.

Abu Rokbeh also said that the implementation of the humanitarian protocol and an urgent increase in aid deliveries to Gaza would be important indicators of a genuine shift in policy.

Some 65 percent of Gaza’s population, about 1.4 million people, live in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN aid coordination office.

Iran’s armed forces chief Ali Abdollahi has warned that the military will “respond without restrictions and beyond the region” if the “enemy” takes action against Iran.

“We will have many surprises for the enemy during the future war. If the Zionist entity makes any mistake against us, we will destroy it,” he said.

The warning follows US President Donald Trump’s declaration on Monday that the war was “effectively over”.

articles.title: The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
articles.summary:
The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics

Submitted by Rikki Sprinzak on Tue, 11/10/2026 - 10:35
Election results expose growing divisions within Haredi society and raise questions about the future of its longstanding alliance with Netanyahu

One of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government. 

This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.

Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.

They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.

This social model developed in Israel, where Torah study in yeshivas and kollelim has become a central way of life and even a social ideal for Haredi men. Many devote years to religious study instead of entering the labour market or undertaking military service. 

The model rests on the belief that Torah study is a supreme value and a communal obligation, supported financially by families, the community, the state and religious support networks.

For decades, the Haredi parties were among the most stable and predictable blocs in Israeli politics. They relied on communal loyalty, rabbinical authority, and the largely automatic voting patterns of a constituency that sought to preserve its political influence through unified Haredi representation.

That model appears to be beginning to fracture. Beyond how many seats each party won in the parliament, or Knesset, the broader question for many is whether Haredi society remains willing to accept its traditional political leadership without question, or is beginning to demand change, accountability and the ability to confront Israel’s changing reality. 

How mass Haredi opposition could reshape Israel
Read More »

The trauma of the Hamas-led 7 October attack may have bypassed the Haredi spiritual leadership and its veteran MPs, but the wider Haredi public, including the generally more conservative Lithuanian community, understands that something momentous has happened in Israel. This is particularly true of the younger generation.

The traditional divisions between Lithuanian, Hasidic and Sephardi Haredim remain important. But new fault lines are emerging: between younger and older generations, between working Haredim and full-time Torah scholars, and between those seeking greater integration into Israeli society and those who fear that any compromise will undermine the Haredi way of life.

Israel’s regional wars, the question of conscripting yeshiva students, mounting economic hardship among Haredi families and growing tensions between the community and those serving in the military have made these divisions increasingly tangible.

For years, securing the legal status of yeshiva students was a central objective of the Haredi parties. It has now become a dangerous political test. The failure to pass legislation exempting them from military service was not simply a parliamentary setback for UTJ. It exposed the limits of Haredi political leaders’ power and the political price their representatives pay when they fail to deliver on promises to voters.

The changing composition of Haredi political leadership is therefore about more than a reshuffling of personnel. It reflects an attempt to address a crisis of confidence, an increasingly diverse constituency and a political landscape in which even the Haredi parties can no longer take traditional voter loyalty for granted.

A new party

The emergence of HaTzibur HaHaredi ("The Haredi Public"), a new Haredi party, is perhaps one of the most significant changes in the Haredi political landscape. Though it won only a tiny number of votes, behind it are rabbis and other influential forces that have broken the longstanding monopoly of established parties over Haredi political representation.

The party seeks to give a voice to Haredim who do not necessarily identify with the agendas of UTJ (Ashkenazi Jews of European origin) or Shas (Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews of Middle Eastern/North African origin), the two parties dominating the Haredi political landscape. 

This includes those who believe the existing leadership is primarily concerned with preserving its own power and political machinery. A growing section of the Haredi public is tired of living in isolation, effectively in ghettos within the state. Many believe the rabbis of the Council of Torah Sages, the community’s supreme ultra-Orthodox rabbinical authority, most of whom are approaching 90 or older, are seeking to impose a future of perpetual isolation and poverty.

These new Haredim, who prefer to call themselves "Israeli Haredim", are advocating a different model. They are raising a fundamental question: can they remain Haredi, preserve their religious and communal identity, and at the same time demand greater integration into Israeli society, greater civic responsibility and a renewed debate about military service?

The party’s emergence presents the traditional leadership with a challenge it has not faced before. Until now, dissatisfied Haredi voters could abstain, support another party or voice their opposition within the community. They now have a political alternative that speaks in a Haredi voice without necessarily accepting the rules of the Haredi establishment.

This does not mean that a new Haredi political camp with substantial electoral strength has emerged. The party’s electoral support remains limited. Nevertheless, its existence could reshape public discourse, bring new issues onto the political agenda and increase pressure on the established parties.

The decision by Dr Nechumi Yaffe, a scholar of Haredi society and political psychology, to join the party and stand as a candidate also signals an effort to broaden Haredi representation beyond the familiar, male-dominated world of political operatives. The change is largely symbolic, but far from insignificant.

Reshuffle

The dramatic removal of Moshe Gafni from the leadership of UTJ was a particularly striking illustration of these developments. Gafni, who had served in the Knesset since 1988 and was long one of the most influential figures in Haredi politics, failed to retain his position.

The official explanation was the need to "refresh" the leadership and bring in new representatives. But the decision reflects a more complex political struggle. The failure to pass legislation exempting yeshiva students from military service, Gafni’s declining influence and the battle for control of the party machinery all contributed to his removal.

The move also exposed a shift in the balance of power within the rabbinical leadership. Rabbi Dov Landau, leader of the Lithuanian Haredi community, and his inner circle sought to ensure greater loyalty from political representatives to the current rabbinical leadership.

Gafni, who had enjoyed considerable independence for years thanks to his experience, connections and political skills, had increasingly become a difficult figure to control.

The removal of MP Uri Maklev alongside Gafni suggests that this was not simply a personal rebuke to the veteran politician. It was part of a broader effort to replace an established generation of politicians and tighten rabbinical control over parliamentary representation.

The decision also reflects a reassessment of the alliance with Netanyahu and the Israeli right. That partnership has carried political costs, including the legitimisation of extreme nationalist positions. It has also contributed to younger Haredi voters shifting their support directly to right-wing parties, particularly Itamar Ben Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit. 

Netanyahu's ultra-Orthodox alliance shows signs of fracture before crucial election
Read More »

Gafni has been replaced by MP Yaakov Asher, who now chairs both Degel HaTorah, one of the main factions of the UTJ, and the alliance overall. A former mayor of Bnei Brak and Knesset member since 2013, Asher is a different kind of political figure. He lacks Gafni’s lengthy parliamentary experience but is regarded as close to and loyal to the Lithuanian rabbinical leadership, particularly Rabbi Dov Landau.

Asher does not necessarily represent a more open approach to changing relations between Haredi society and the state.

However, his record as chairman of the Knesset Interior Committee has earned him praise for his accessibility and ability to build alliances across different groups. These are skills that the veteran Gafni appeared to have lost.

Against the backdrop of a growing, more modern and economically active Haredi public that does not necessarily identify with the traditional leadership, Asher’s remarks in an interview with the Haredi news website Kikar HaShabbat last month were particularly significant.

He explicitly stated that he sees himself as representing both full-time Torah scholars and working Haredim. This is an important message to the younger Haredi generation.

On military conscription, however, Asher takes a hard line. He even resigned as chairman of the Interior Committee in protest at the failure to regulate the status of yeshiva students. Nevertheless, his experience as mayor of the Haredi city of Bnei Brak may give him a practical understanding of both the community’s needs and the workings of government. 

The question is whether he can combine these practical skills with his uncompromising position on Haredi conscription.

What is clear is that representatives of the Ashkenazi Haredi community have skilfully positioned themselves as potential partners for both political camps. 

UTJ abstained from recommending a candidate for prime minister during consultations with President Isaac Herzog. This has left both Gadi Eisenkot, who has been given a month to form a government, and Netanyahu courting the party’s support.

Shas’ crisis of identity

While UTJ is undergoing a major leadership upheaval, the latest election results reveal a different and more acute crisis within Shas, the Sephardi Haredi party: a crisis of identity and representation.

The results dealt the party a severe blow. Shas fell from a peak of 11 seats in the 2022 elections to just six, losing nearly 100,000 votes. The scale of the defeat prompted longtime leader Aryeh Deri to resign. However, the Shas Council of Torah Sages rejected his resignation, prompting him to give up his Knesset seat while retaining his position as party chairman.

Over the past few years, Deri has made several serious political miscalculations. He followed the Lithuanian Haredi leadership’s hard line on military conscription and failed to position himself as a bridge between Haredi society and secular Israelis.

Shas was founded not simply as a Sephardi Haredi party, but as a social and political movement. It gave a voice to a large constituency of Mizrahi and traditional Jews who felt excluded from the centres of power in Israeli society.

Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, the party’s legendary spiritual leader and founder, succeeded in bringing together two worlds: Sephardi Torah scholarship and the wider traditional Jewish public. For many, Shas was more than a political party. It represented identity, dignity and belonging. 

After Rabbi Ovadia’s death, Deri managed to preserve the party’s strength, but its centre of gravity gradually shifted. Shas became increasingly identified with Haredi coalition politics and its alliance with Netanyahu.

This may help explain the election results. Haredi voters felt that Shas was not sufficiently Haredi, while traditional voters, many of whom had served in the military, believed it had become too Haredi. They rejected Deri’s position on conscription.

Shas is now caught between two constituencies that once formed the foundation of its strength: a Sephardi Haredi public seeking to protect the world of Torah study, and a broader traditional constituency demanding social representation, economic mobility and a sense of belonging to the state.

The fall to six seats does not necessarily spell the end of Shas. But it confronts Deri with a fundamental strategic question: will the party continue to prioritise its position within the Haredi leadership, or seek to return to its roots as a broad social movement that also represents traditional Jews beyond the Haredi establishment?

Shas recommended Netanyahu to Herzog as its candidate to form the next government. Ultimately, however, its MPs are likely to support whichever government UTJ, the Ashkenazi Haredi party, and its spiritual leader, Rabbi Landau, decide to back.

What next?

It remains to be seen whether Eisenkot can reach an agreement with Haredi parties to form the next government, ending their almost 17-year-long alliance with Netanyahu. 

What is clear, however, is that Haredi society is undergoing several contradictory processes simultaneously.

On the one hand, the rabbinical leadership is seeking to tighten its control over politicians, as demonstrated by the removal of Gafni and Maklev and the appointment of Asher to lead the UJT. On the other hand, there is growing recognition that Haredi society can no longer remain detached from the central issues facing Israel: military service, employment, education, the economy and relations between Haredi and secular Jews.

The latest elections do not yet represent a victory for those seeking change within Haredi society. The new party failed to enter the Knesset, while the established leadership retains its grip on religious and political power.

Yet the younger generation is growing up in a very different reality. Most own smartphones and have access to the internet. They are increasingly exposed to wider Israeli society, face rising living costs and growing concerns about their economic future, and live in a security environment in which military service is anything but an abstract question.

Many remain committed to Torah study, but that does not mean they automatically accept every decision made by their political leaders.

Why are ultra-Orthodox Jews against conscription?
Read More »

Decades ago, Professor Menachem Friedman, one of the pioneers of research into Haredi society, identified an inherent contradiction in the "society of learners" model. He described how, after the Holocaust, rebuilding the yeshiva world became a central Haredi undertaking. 

Full-time Torah study gradually evolved from an ideal pursued by a select few into an all-encompassing social norm. Friedman warned that a model dependent on a growing proportion of men not working to support their families could not be sustained indefinitely.

“This is a situation that cannot continue,” he said in a 2012 interview.

Today, for the first time, such criticism is also coming from within Haredi politics. Moti Leitner, chairman of HaTzibur HaHaredi, goes beyond opposing the exemption from military service. He challenges the very economic and social foundations of the society of learners, arguing that the model is collapsing and no longer reflects the realities of many within the Haredi community.

The UTJ’s refusal to recommend Netanyahu may ultimately prove to be little more than another tactical manoeuvre in coalition negotiations. But viewed alongside Gafni’s removal, the leadership changes in UTJ, Shas’s declining electoral strength and the emergence of a new Haredi party, it points to a broader transformation.

Haredi society is not yet undergoing a revolution, and conservative forces continue to dominate its centres of authority. Beneath the surface, however, a fundamental debate is taking shape over the very meaning of Haredi identity, the relationship between Torah and the state, military service and employment, and, ultimately, who has the right to speak on behalf of the Haredi public.

articles.title: The sum of the humanitarian paradigm is deadly
articles.summary: The discrepancy between what the international community glorifies as humanitarian aid and what Gaza is deprived of keep growing. A woman and four children were killed following heavy rains in Gaza which caused a landslide at the site in Deir al-Balah where displaced Palestinians are living in tents that offer no protection from winter storms. archive.security_status_cs: Izraelská politická scéna čelí hluboké krizi po volbách, kdy opozice usiluje o sestavení vlády bez Netanjahua a čelí obviněním z delegitimizace výsledků.
